name: two-level scrap shack seen from above: a small upper room with a blue tarp roof and its own front wall with a window sits on the back of the flat plywood roof of the lower room, the lower roof forms a walkable deck in front of it with a short rail, a wooden ladder leans on the lower front wall of rusty sheets and planks with a door

surfaces.part: short rail and ladder on deck

answer.evidence: The lower room has a wide plywood deck (rows 8-28 at the left, rows 23-28 in front of the upper room). It ends in a light front-edge line at row 29 (#ddbf91) and dark eave shadow at rows 30-31. Below it is a 15-row front face (rows 32-46) with a door, a window, and rusty sheets and planks. The upper room has its own blue tarp roof (rows 0-8) with a light edge line at row 9 and shadow at rows 10-11, above its front wall with a window and door (rows 12-22). Both volumes show a top surface and a front face. No isometric side face is drawn.

styleAnswer.evidence: The measured facts are close to the references: 11 visible tones per tile against 12 and 10, and 0% neutral dark edges, so the outline is tinted. The picture shows a shallower build. The candidate is tiny next to the references, and its main materials (plywood deck, blue tarp, rusty wall, planks) mostly have 2-3 steps each, where the references carry 5-6 on roof tiles, plaster and stone. Their per-tile scallops, stone-by-stone shading and plaster speckle are mostly absent here. There is some grain on the planks and sheet panels, but the deck and the lower wall still read as large, fairly flat fills (11% near-flat coverage against 0% for both references). The rail, ladder and window are readable but thin. Structure and outline are acceptable, but the shading depth and texture richness are below the Beodeul bar, so it fails.

Its measured facts are close to the references: 11 visible tones per tile against 10-12, and 0% neutral dark edge pixels, so the outlines carry a tint. By eye they are dark brown beside wood and dark blue beside the tarp, which makes them dark_material_tone rather than a black sticker line. The shading is where it falls short. The plywood deck, the wall planks and the tarp each show only about 3 lightness steps, where the references use 5-6 per material (roof tiles with per-tile highlights, stone shaded one by one, plaster speckle). The rusty sheets have some variation, and the tarp and window clutter add some detail, but the tile-by-tile craft of the references is missing. On balance it is flatter and shallower than the references, so with doubt it fails.
